issues.claim: Pilot software cost of "$0-$150/month in software (zero if using Frigate's local LPR only; about $45 per camera per month if using Plate Recognizer Stream)"
issues.problem: Internal arithmetic inconsistency: the pilot specifies 3-4 cameras, and Plate Recognizer Stream is $45 per camera per month, so the paid fallback is $135-$180/month, not capped at $150.
issues.fix: Change the ceiling to about $180/month for four cameras, or state the per-camera multiplier explicitly.

issues.problem: The numbers are correct and peer-reviewed, but this is one paper on one dataset (4,000 images, six classes), i.e. a single study used to bound the whole technical feasibility argument. The role rule is that a single study should not be rated High.
issues.fix: Rate Medium-High or Medium, or state that the finding is a single-dataset benchmark result rather than an outcome measured in the field.

issues.claim: measured_outcomes: "Even a purpose-built ALPR system on the UFPR-ALPR benchmark read only 64.89% ... commercial systems scored 47.39% and 50.94%"
issues.problem: Accurate as stated (single-frame, all-characters-correct), but one-sided and decontextualised: the same table shows the commercial systems reach 56.67% and 70.00% with temporal redundancy, and the dataset is Brazilian plates with both camera and vehicle moving, which is not the shop-lane case the brief uses it to argue.
issues.fix: Add the with-redundancy commercial figures and note the dataset is Brazilian plates / moving camera, then say why the shop-lane case is easier (static camera, vehicle slows or stops).

issues.claim: problem.summary: "Shops almost never measure bay occupancy or per-vehicle dwell time, because doing so means a person with a clipboard."
issues.problem: Stated as fact with no source. Nothing fetched supports the frequency claim, and the brief's own data_gaps concedes no study of shop bay-occupancy measurement was found.
issues.fix: Label as inference/assumption, or drop the frequency claim and keep only the mechanism (measurement is manual today).

issues.claim: gap_for_local_installer: "UVeye itself says a ~100-car/month shop is not a fit, which is most of the 233 general repair shops in the county"
issues.problem: The UVeye quote is confirmed, but "most of the 233 general repair shops" is an inference stated as fact; the trailing "(inference)" label is attached to the following sentence about defensibility, not to this one.
issues.fix: Move the (inference) tag or rephrase as "plausibly most of the 233 ... (inference; QCEW gives no volume distribution)".

issues.claim: legal_privacy row 3: "License plate reading on a shop's own lot is not governed by NJ's police ALPR rules, which apply to law enforcement agencies only" — marked confirmed: true
issues.problem: The directive's content is confirmed (law-enforcement purposes only, public-view scanning, three-year retention, three purposes for non-alert data, private entities may provide but not receive), but the step from "the directive binds agencies" to "a private shop is not governed" is an inference from the text, not something the directive states.
issues.fix: Set confirmed: false for the private-shop conclusion while keeping the directive's provisions as confirmed, consistent with the treatment of the P.L. 2026 c.4 row.

issues.claim: prospecting_signals.public: NJ MVC auto body "$300,000 garage liability / $50,000 garage-keepers' limits ... I confirmed those figures only via search summary of the MVC page, not by reading the page"
issues.problem: Over-cautious, not wrong. I opened https://www.nj.gov/mvc/business/autobodylic.htm myself and both figures and the per-location application rule are stated there verbatim.
issues.fix: Upgrade to a directly read, cited page (MVC Auto Body Repair License page) and drop the hedge.

issues.claim: fit_score.rationale: "the trade press describes shops as 'wait and see'"
issues.problem: Quote drift. The source phrase is "the wait-and-see skepticism of later adopters"; it is not a standalone quoted phrase.
issues.fix: Paraphrase ("characterised as wait-and-see adopters") or quote the actual wording.

issues.claim: buyers: body shop "why": "(67% of repairs get a supplement)"
issues.problem: The 67% is correct but drops the qualifier used elsewhere in the brief: it is CCC collision/insurance-claim industrywide data, not all repairs at all shop types.
issues.fix: Add "(CCC collision-claims data)" so the mechanical-repair reader is not misled.

N.J.S.A. 56:8-19 per Sylince v. Thrift Auto Sales (App. Div., Docket A-5891-13T1, 2015): once unlawful conduct, ascertainable loss and causation are proven, "treble damages and counsel fees ... are mandatory" and the trial court has "no discretion to deny this relief"
67% of all repairs include at least one supplement, up from 57% in 2019; supplements about 22.5% of total repair cost (18% in 2019, 10% in 2009), per CCC industrywide data

Tom Wood Group reported 29.3% of vehicles through its scan lane had something the owner did not know about; the same article notes the AI system did not at the time find some ADAS sensor damage
BayWatch had 500 units on order before tariff turmoil
Shopmonkey published tiers at $239, $399 and $499 per month, with slightly lower annual pricing ($215/$359/$449) and custom enterprise pricing
Plate Recognizer Stream at $45 per camera per month, a $35 3-camera one-month trial tier, Snapshot lookup plans from $50/month, and $500 per professional-services session

Frigate docs recommend Hailo-8/Hailo-8L m.2 modules or an Intel iGPU with OpenVINO, and state the Google Coral is no longer recommended for new installations

NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super Developer Kit at $249, down from $499, 67 INT8 TOPS
Amcrest 5MP PoE bullet camera IP5M-B1186EW (white) listed at $79.99, out of stock at retrieval

CarDD: 4,000 images, 9,000+ annotations, six classes; best model (DCN+, ResNet-101) reaches 57.0 mask AP / 60.6 box AP, 77.7 / 78.8 at IoU 0.50, with per-class box AP 39.2 dent, 36.6 scratch, 30.6 crack, 91.2 glass shatter, 86.4 tire flat; published IEEE T-ITS 2023

UFPR-ALPR: the proposed system read 64.89% of plates fully correct per frame, 78.33% with temporal redundancy; the two commercial baselines scored 47.39% and 50.94% (all correct, single frame); 150 videos, 4,500 frames, camera and vehicle both moving
71% of the alerts Flock Safety's AI plate readers sent to Roseville, CA police over two years were misreads, incorrectly flagging vehicles as stolen or felony-linked

In a survey of 500 US independent repair shops (fielded December 2023), 56% named finding qualified/responsible technicians as a 2024 challenge and 27.2% named retaining them; for shops with eight or more bays retention was the second-largest concern at 43.2%

AG Law Enforcement Directive 2022-12 (eff. Jan 23, 2023) applies to law enforcement: scanning limited to plates exposed to public view, three-year retention, stored non-alert data limited to three purposes, and private entities "may provide ALPR data to New Jersey agencies but cannot receive law enforcement-owned ALPR data"
